name: Amla oil

card.summary: A traditional Ayurvedic hair oil made by infusing Indian gooseberry in a carrier oil, used to condition hair and scalp for shinier, fuller-looking hair.
card.aka: Indian gooseberry oil; amla hair oil; amla taila; amalaki taila
card.note: Rare reports of irritation or pigmentation; patch testing is commonly advised.

quick.overview:
Amla oil is an Ayurvedic preparation in which the fruit of Phyllanthus emblica, the Indian gooseberry, is infused into a carrier oil such as coconut or sesame. It is massaged into hair and scalp as a conditioning treatment.

Users apply it for shine, softness, less breakage and a healthier scalp, and traditional sources also credit it with supporting hair growth and delaying greying. Lab and animal studies have examined hair-growth and anti-dandruff effects, while human trials mostly used extracts rather than the infused oil.
quick.how: Traditionally the oil is warmed, massaged into the scalp and hair, left on for anywhere from half an hour to overnight and then washed out with a mild cleanser, in a weekly routine.
quick.risks: Topical use is described as generally well tolerated, with rare mild irritation. Rare cases of lichen planus pigmentosus have been linked to amla oil in predisposed people, so patch testing on the forearm is commonly recommended.

lead: Amla oil, also called Indian gooseberry oil or amla taila, is a traditional Ayurvedic hair oil made by infusing the fruit of Phyllanthus emblica in a carrier oil such as coconut or sesame. It is distinct from pure amla seed oil, which is pressed from the seeds.[1]

People use it to condition the scalp and hair. Traditional uses credit it with promoting growth, strengthening roots, reducing breakage, adding shine, delaying greying and easing dandruff.[1] Hair oils like it are used across India: a survey cited in a 1992 study found amla oil used equally by men and women.[2]

Research includes a 1992 laboratory study in which amla oil inhibited the growth of several skin fungi, a 2012 enzyme study in which the plant inhibited 5-alpha reductase, and small human trials of amla extracts.[1][2]

chain: Oil massaged into scalp and hair
Conditions hair and supports a healthy scalp
Shinier, less brittle hair; claimed thicker growth
angle.text: The oil coats and softens hair, giving shine and reducing breakage, which many users say makes hair look fuller. Growth and greying claims come from tradition and early research.

paras: Traditional preparation simmers dried amla pieces or a decoction of amla powder in a carrier oil over low heat until the water has evaporated. Regional variants use coconut oil in Kerala and mustard oil in northern traditions.[1]

Hair care claims include growth, strengthening, shine, less breakage, delayed greying and dandruff relief.[1] Amla is also eaten as a food and used in Ayurvedic formulations; the fruit is rich in vitamin C and tannins.[3]

A 1992 study found amla oil inhibited several dermatophyte species, and for some it was more toxic to the fungi than coconut oil.[2] Grokipedia summarises further work: a 2012 study ranking the plant among those inhibiting 5-alpha reductase, a mouse study of an amla-containing formulation showing regrowth comparable to 3% minoxidil, and human trials of an oral syrup (60 women), a topical serum (42 adults) and a formulation versus placebo, which reported improved hair measures.[1] Most human studies used extracts or oral products rather than the infused oil.[1]
The human trials listed above used amla extracts, syrups or serums and reported improvements in hair-growth measures; trials of the traditional infused oil are scarce.[1]

A 2016 case report listed amla oil among rare exposures reported in lichen planus pigmentosus, a pigmentation condition.[4] Guidance usually suggests patch testing and stopping if irritation develops.[1]
